## The puzzle

```{=html}
<div class="concise-only">
```

Hormuz throughput collapsed from 138 daily transits to 4 (a 97% reduction). Trump declined the 16 March Saudi/UAE call to fully reopen. He released only 22.7 mb from the SPR (Biden released 180 mb in 2022 over a Russian-oil shock of ~10% magnitude). Is the US structurally interested in keeping Hormuz partially blocked — because the US is now the world's largest oil and LNG producer, and each $10/b Brent uplift is worth ~$50bn/yr to US producers? Or is this just Trump's coalition, not a structural feature of the US polity?

```{=html}
</div>
<div class="deep-only">
```

After 28 February 2026, Hormuz throughput collapsed from 138 daily transits to 4 — a 97% reduction. Trump declined the 16 March Saudi/UAE call to fully reopen the Strait. The Trump administration released only 22.7 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve between 27 February and 1 May 2026 — for comparison, Biden released 180 million barrels in 2022 over a much smaller Russian-oil shock (~10% magnitude). Operation Project Freedom (4 May+) restored escort operations and partial commercial transit but was deliberately bounded; the dual blockade (Western on Iran, Iranian on Hormuz) continues. Meanwhile US shale producers are *expanding* drilling capacity in the Permian; LNG export terminals are running at design throughput; US LNG is now ~60% of EU imports. The structural claim: the US — as the world's largest oil and LNG producer — has a *structural* interest in Hormuz *not* returning to pre-war flow levels. Each $10/b sustained Brent uplift yields ~$50bn/year to US oil sector revenue. The Asian buyer dependence on US LNG deepens. The strategic-rivalry containment of CRINK tightens. Is this a structural feature of the post-shale US polity — or is it Trump's coalition specifically, reversible on administration change? The 2022 Biden case is the load-bearing test.

::: {.bottom-line}
**Bottom line.** *Qualified yes (weak-form), administration-contingent within a structural envelope (P ≈ 0.55).* Two load-bearing mechanisms: **α** [Grossman-Helpman lobby-weight]{.gloss data-gloss="grossman-helpman-lobby"} — Trump-admin producer-coalition dominance reflects domestic political economy, not structural relocation. **β** [Kelanic-inverted command-of-commons]{.gloss data-gloss="kelanic-command-of-commons"} + [Krasner-HST Saudi-exporter exception]{.gloss data-gloss="krasner-hegemonic-stability"} — sets the strategic envelope within which producer-side options are strategically permissible. The 2022 Biden case (180 mb SPR; identical structural status) is the base-rate killer for the strong-form. Reversible on administration change.
:::

::: {.bottom-line}
**Bottom line.** *Qualified yes with administration-contingent framing (P ≈ 0.55).* The weak-form claim — Trump-admin producer-coalition dominance is currently operative — holds. The strong-form claim — US polity has *structurally relocated* to producer-side interest regardless of admin — is **rejected** (P ≈ 0.25, capped by the 2022 Biden base-rate disconfirmer). Two load-bearing mechanisms operating simultaneously. **α — [Grossman-Helpman lobby-weight]{.gloss data-gloss="grossman-helpman-lobby"} dominance under Trump admin specifically**: the government's revealed objective function *v⁰ = ΣA_i(p) + α·W(p)* has low α-weight on aggregate consumer welfare; producer-coalition contributions (Permian operators, LNG exporters, oil-state Senate caucus) dominate. P(operative) = 0.80; P(load-bearing for policy choice) = 0.60. **β — [Kelanic-inverted command-of-commons]{.gloss data-gloss="kelanic-command-of-commons"} + [Krasner-HST Saudi-exporter exception]{.gloss data-gloss="krasner-hegemonic-stability"}**: post-shale net-exporter status creates a structural envelope within which producer-side options are strategically permissible (US can sustain disruption without inviting coercive response from rivals). P(operative) = 0.85; P(load-bearing for envelope) = 0.40. **α determines policy choice; β sets the feasible set.** The 2022 Biden case is the base-rate disconfirmer for strong-form: under identical US net-exporter status, Biden chose consumer-side (180 mb SPR; aggressive Saudi production diplomacy; Russian-oil price-cap rather than embargo). Six load-bearing T3 inferences cap the posterior at ≤ 0.55 per META rule 5. Q10 is the third principled-multi-framework case in the project (after Q7 and Q9) — the framework-domain mapping (Grossman-Helpman domestic political economy × Krasner-Kelanic international structural position) is *literature-derived* and pre-analysis, not Lakatos rescue.

## Methodology — Tier-2 abbreviated protocol + the BIDIRECTIONAL META rule 7 test

This chapter applies the Tier-2 abbreviated protocol: pre-Q corpus audit, three new acquisitions (Krasner 1976, Kelanic 2020, Grossman-Helpman 1994), steel-mans A/B/C written in-house, the seven META rules applied throughout. No separate multi-agent DA cycle; META rule discipline substitutes. The most consequential moves: META rule 2 (base-rate) catches the 2022 Biden disconfirmer that kills strong-form; META rule 3 (currently-dominant vs structurally-locked-in) forces the weak-form finding; META rule 4 (mechanism reduction) collapses six candidates to two; META rule 6 (no refinement rescue) subsumes the partial-disruption hypothesis under weak-form. Q10 also applies the BIDIRECTIONAL form of META rule 7 (generated by Q9): test unitary alternatives *before* defaulting to multi-framework. No single framework covers both the domestic-political-economy axis (admin variation) and the international-structural-position axis (US net-exporter + command-of-commons). The multi-framework finding is principled (literature-derived domains), not rescue.
:::

[**The base-rate killer.** 2022 Biden under identical US net-exporter status: 180 mb SPR release (largest in US history), aggressive Saudi production pressure (the July 2022 fist-bump trip), Russian-oil price-cap rather than embargo. 2026 Trump: 22.7 mb SPR (~12% the size), declined Saudi/UAE Hormuz-opening call, sustained dual blockade. Same structural status; opposite revealed policy. *Strong-form is dead.*]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**The base-rate killer for strong-form.** META rule 2 (base-rate analysis) requires an explicit comparison case. The 2022 Russia-Ukraine response is the load-bearing case: same US net-exporter structural status; opposite admin policy choice. *Biden's revealed wartime energy policy (March-October 2022)*: 180 million barrel SPR release — the largest in US history, 1 million barrels per day for six months; aggressive Saudi production diplomacy including Biden's July 2022 fist-bump Riyadh visit pressing MBS for ramp-up; initially declined Russian-oil sanctions; eventually opted for a Russian-oil price-cap rather than embargo because of price concerns. Net effect: Brent peaked at $128/b in March 2022 (the 2026 Iran war reached an identical $128/b peak on 2 April); Biden's response was *price-suppressive*. Trump's response in 2026 is *price-permissive*. *The strong-form's prediction "any US admin under net-exporter status would pursue producer-side wartime policy" is empirically false.* The 22.7 mb 2026 SPR release is ~12% the size of Biden's 2022 release for a war that has produced a 97% Hormuz reduction (vs Biden's ~10% Russian-oil shock). The base-rate inference: P(admin choosing producer-side | net-exporter + war + Republican with oil-state coalition) ≈ 0.75; P(admin choosing producer-side | net-exporter + war + Democratic) ≈ 0.20. The admin variable dominates the structural variable in observed revealed preference. Confounders aside (2026 has higher peak severity, higher CRINK rivalry stakes, higher producer-coalition political weight in admin), no plausible counterfactual has Biden 2022 sustaining a 97% Hormuz blockade while declining ally restoration requests.
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage3"}
[**Mechanism α — [Grossman-Helpman lobby-weight]{.gloss data-gloss="grossman-helpman-lobby"} dominance under Trump admin.** The government's revealed objective is *v⁰ = ΣA_i(p) + α·W(p)*. α_Trump ≪ α_Biden. The α parameter is *exogenous* in this period (set by election results, coalition composition); endogenous over longer horizons. Predicts: Trump admin sustains disruption while consumer-coalition mobilization is below threshold (gasoline national average < $4.50/gal sustained 60 days).]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**Mechanism α — [Grossman-Helpman lobby-weight]{.gloss data-gloss="grossman-helpman-lobby"} dominance under Trump admin specifically.** The formal apparatus: the government's revealed policy objective is *v⁰ = ΣA_i(p) + α·W(p)* where v⁰ is the government's revealed objective function, A_i(p) is the contribution schedule from organized interest group i (here: producer coalition — Permian operators, LNG exporters, oil-state Senate caucus), W(p) is aggregate welfare of voters (here: consumer coalition, diffuse), and α is the weight government attaches to aggregate welfare relative to net valuation of contributions. *Trump 2026 has α_Trump ≪ α_Biden.* Producer-coalition contributions dominate the revealed-policy function. Biden 2022 had α_Biden ≫ α_Trump — consumer-coalition concerns (gasoline-price politics, electoral consequence) dominated. The α parameter is exogenous to the model in this period (set by election results, coalition composition); it is endogenous over longer horizons (lobby-weight investments shape future α). *Predictions (operationalized)*: Trump admin sustains Hormuz disruption while consumer-coalition mobilization remains below threshold (gasoline national average < $4.50/gal). If gasoline national average sustains > $4.50/gal for 60+ days, expect partial pivot (SPR release acceleration; Saudi production pressure). A Democratic admin succeeding Trump (2029) under similar structural conditions would pivot to consumer-side; the reversal would take 6-12 months due to producer-coalition investment path-dependence. Posterior: P(operative) = 0.80; P(load-bearing for Q10 policy choice) = 0.60. Three load-bearing T3 inferences.
:::
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage4"}
[**Mechanism β — Structural envelope.** [Kelanic-inverted command-of-commons]{.gloss data-gloss="kelanic-command-of-commons"} (US uniquely invulnerable; chief military threat) + [Krasner Saudi-exporter exception]{.gloss data-gloss="krasner-hegemonic-stability"} (large reserves reduce opportunity cost of closure) set the *envelope* within which producer-side options are strategically permissible. **β does NOT determine policy choice** — that's α's job. β determines the feasible set.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**Mechanism β — International structural envelope from US post-2018 net-exporter status + command-of-commons.** Formal apparatus: [Kelanic 2020]{.gloss data-gloss="kelanic-command-of-commons"} on the US's unique invulnerability to oil coercion (command-of-commons makes the US the chief military threat to other states' oil access, not a target of such threats); [Krasner 1976]{.gloss data-gloss="krasner-hegemonic-stability"} on hegemons' preferences depending on relative power × four state goals, with the explicit Saudi-exporter exception when reserves dramatically reduce the opportunity cost of closure. *Application to Q10*: US 2026 satisfies the Saudi-exporter-exception structural condition — large reserves + production capability + command-of-commons + LNG export leverage. The "hegemon prefers openness" prediction (Krasner default) is *reversed* for the energy-system subdomain. The strategic envelope set: US can sustain Hormuz disruption without inviting coercive response from rivals (no rival has the naval reach to retaliate against US continental positions); US can absorb its own consumer-side political costs because of fiscal capacity; US can offer LNG/oil to disrupted allies, deepening dependency. *This mechanism does NOT determine policy choice* — β does not select between Trump and Biden revealed preferences. β sets the outer envelope of feasibility. *Predictions (operationalized)*: the envelope is binding when consumer-side mobilization fully exceeds producer-coalition weight; even then, full restoration is not pursued because of CRINK strategic stakes. The envelope contracts if (a) US net-exporter status reverses (low probability 2026-30; rising 2030+) or (b) command-of-commons erodes (e.g., A2/AD parity from PLA Navy by 2035). Within the envelope, admin variation determines policy; the envelope itself is structurally stable on a 5-10 year horizon. Posterior: P(operative) = 0.85; P(load-bearing for envelope) = 0.40. Two load-bearing T3 inferences. **α and β are NOT additive on policy choice.** α is the *selection* mechanism (within envelope); β is the *bounding* mechanism (envelope edges). Both simultaneously operative; one determines outcome, the other determines feasible set.
:::

[The mechanism interaction is the load-bearing analytical move. α and β operate simultaneously but serve different functions. α — Grossman-Helpman lobby-weight — is the *selection* mechanism: it determines what policy choice the administration makes from the available options. β — Kelanic-inverted + Krasner Saudi-exporter exception — is the *bounding* mechanism: it determines which options are strategically permissible at all. The structural envelope is what makes Trump's producer-side choice *feasible*; it does not make the choice *necessary*. Under a Democratic administration with a different α, the same envelope would permit consumer-side policy (the Biden 2022 case). The strong-form claim — "US polity has structurally relocated such that any admin would choose producer-side" — would require β to *force* the choice, not merely permit it. The 2022 Biden disconfirmer shows β does not force the choice. The weak-form survives; the strong-form does not.]{.deep-only}

## Pre-mortem {#pre-mortem}

The most likely ways the analysis will be wrong:

1. **Underestimating producer-coalition durability** (P ≈ 0.20). The Permian financial sector + oil-state Senate caucus has lobby-weight α-effect that persists across admin changes — Democratic admins from 2029+ feel similar pressure. Weak-form is wrong and a strengthened weak-form (or even strong-form) is correct.

2. **Misreading Biden 2022 case** (P ≈ 0.20). Biden 2022 was actually responding to recession-risk concerns (the envelope's hard edge from β) rather than consumer-coalition lobby-weight (α). The admin variation is illusory — it's the same mechanism (envelope binding) firing under different parameters.

3. **CRINK containment is the actually-load-bearing mechanism, not producer-coalition** (P ≈ 0.25). The Trump admin's revealed preference is primarily about CRINK strategic-rivalry containment rather than producer-revenue. The signature would be Trump admin sustaining Hormuz pressure even after gasoline prices fully normalize (i.e., even after α-mechanism would have predicted pivot).

4. **Partial-disruption hypothesis was right** (P ≈ 0.15). The subsumption may be premature. If Trump admin actively moderates throughput at specific levels (e.g., explicit calls for restoring 50% of pre-war flow), the partial-preference framing is the actual mechanism.

5. **The 2022/2026 cases are not comparable** (P ≈ 0.20). Structural conditions differ enough that the base-rate inference fails (2022 Russian-oil shock was 10% vs 2026 Hormuz at 97%; admin response under 97% scenario could be uniform across parties). Strong-form revives.

**Total probability the finding is substantively wrong**: ≈ 0.40 (with overlap; not strictly additive). Consistent with the META-rule-5-capped posterior of 0.55.

## Pre-1979 historical lineage

The Q10 question — whether the US has a *structural* interest in Hormuz NOT returning to pre-war flow levels — has a 70-year prehistory that strengthens the β-envelope finding. The genealogical origin of US producer interest in Persian Gulf flows is the **1954 IOP consortium**: BP 40%, Royal Dutch Shell 14%, **five US majors at 8% each** (Standard Oil of California, Standard Oil of New Jersey, Standard Oil of New York, Texaco, Gulf), CFP 6%. This structure was negotiated *immediately after* the 1953 CIA-MI6 coup that removed Mosaddegh; it gave Iran the 50/50 deal AIOC had previously refused, and gave US majors operational entry to the Iranian oil sector for the first time at scale. The earlier 1924 Imbrie killing (a mob in Tehran killed Robert Imbrie, eliminating the Sinclair Oil concession) had foreclosed US oil entry for thirty years; the 1953 coup reopened it.

The deeper substrate runs to the 1901 D'Arcy Concession (60 years tax-free for £40,000 + 16% of "net profit" calculated by the concessionaire), the 1908 founding of APOC, Churchill's 1914 Admiralty purchase making the *British government* the concession holder, and the 1933 AIOC revision that extended the concession to 1993. The 1954 IOP consortium structure made Iran a definitively oil-rentier state. **The 2026 oil situation is the third act of a story whose first two acts were the 1901 D'Arcy Concession and the 1953 coup.** Trump's revealed preference for sustained Hormuz disruption operates on producer-coalition lobby weight (α), but the *structural envelope* (β) that makes this preference operationally feasible has a 70-year prehistory: command of the commons is older than the post-shale net-exporter status; the Saudi-exporter exception Krasner identified in 1976 was operationalized in the IOP framework in 1954.

**Full pre-1979 context**: [Historical roots](../historical-roots/index.qmd).
